patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch improves the handling of MADV_PAGEOUT folios on asynchronous swap devices by marking them as dropbehind at isolation time instead of waiting for writeback completion. This allows the memory to be freed earlier, reducing latency and improving performance. The patch also updates various kernel modules to handle the new behavior correctly.

But we have the same behavior when just reclaiming memory ordinarily? It's added

review_comments.author: Barry Song
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer noted that the patch does not handle the case where a folio is already under writeback, and suggested adding a check to ensure that the folio is not being written back before marking it as dropbehind.

Reviewer Barry Song noted that the current implementation of MADV_PAGEOUT for asynchronous I/O, which delays folio release until a later scan, can lead to cold/hot inversion due to NVMe's fast writeback completion during isolation. He pointed out that this issue is similar to one addressed by Ridong's patch for active/inactive LRU reclaim path and suggested considering skipping the later scan and reclaiming folios immediately once I/O completes.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Mon, Sep 21, 2026 at 11:37 PM David Hildenbrand (Arm)
<david@kernel.org> wrote:

---

For synchronous I/O, such as zswap and zram, the memory is released
immediately after sync I/O is done.

For asynchronous I/O, such as NVMe, the swapcache is currently
expected to be rotated back to the tail of the LRU and wait for
another scan. Alexandre once mentioned that when he tried handling
async I/O the same way as sync I/O—releasing the memory once the I/O
completed—he saw some regression. So, delaying the release until a
later scan may allow swapcache hits before the folios are eventually
reclaimed.

But we actually have a problem here: this rotation, which puts
writeback folios at the tail of the LRU, is not reliable at all.

`folio_rotate_reclaimable()` would only work reliably if the endio
happens after the folio has been put back on the LRU head, rather than
while it is still isolated.

But nowadays NVMe is very fast. If we isolate N pages and perform
shrink on them, M pages may finish writeback during the isolation,
while the remaining N-M pages are still under writeback. M can easily
be more than 50% of N.

As a result, we can end up with the following cold/hot inversion:

LRU head
----- M pages whose writeback completed during isolation
----- other pages
----- N-M pages that are successfully rotated to the LRU tail
LRU tail

Now we can see that the M pages were expected to be reclaimed, but
they are not only left unreclaimed, but are effectively promoted to
the LRU head.

For MGLRU, commit 359a5e1416ca ("mm: multi-gen LRU: retry folios
written back while isolated") added the following code to reclaim
those M pages that finish writeback during isolation by retrying
`shrink_folio_list()` on them:

                /* retry folios that may have missed
folio_rotate_reclaimable() */
                if (!skip_retry && !folio_test_active(folio) &&
!folio_mapped(folio) &&
                    !folio_test_dirty(folio) && !folio_test_writeback(folio)) {
                        list_move(&folio->lru, &clean);
                        continue;
                }

This somehow resolves the cold/hot inversion, but leaves the M and
N-M pages with inconsistent behavior: some are actually reclaimed,
while others remain at the tail of the LRU.

For the active/inactive LRU and `MADV_PAGEOUT`, we don't have a
mechanism to restore the missed reclaim opportunity. Ridong's patch[1]
addresses this cold/hot inversion in the active/inactive LRU reclaim
path. To my knowledge, there has never been a patch to address the
same cold/hot inversion in `MADV_PAGEOUT`.

BTW, if `MADV_PAGEOUT` is an explicit hint from userspace to reclaim
the memory, would it make sense to skip the later scan and reclaim the
folios immediately once the I/O completes?

[1] https://lore.kernel.org/linux-mm/20260920132519.3369946-1-ridong.chen@linux.dev/

Best Regards
Barry

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 1/3] mm: swap: move LRU insertion out of the swap cache allocator
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the insertion of a new folio into the LRU out of the swap cache allocator, allowing callers to act on the folio before it becomes visible to reclaim. This is necessary for two use cases: moving refault evaluation out of the allocation and zswap writeback dropbehind. The helper function is renamed from `swap_cache_alloc_folio` to `__swap_cache_alloc_folio`, and its callers are responsible for adding the folio to the LRU after allocation.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 2/3] mm: swap: drop dropbehind swap cache folios on writeback completion
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the Linux kernel to drop swap cache folios from their cache once writeback completes, rather than leaving them for reclaim later. This is done by adding a new function `swap_writeback_dropbehind_folio` that drops the folio directly from `folio_end_writeback`. The change ensures that the folio is not left in the swap cache with no way to reclaim it, and prevents blocking on the folio lock in interrupt context. The patch also updates several other functions to handle dropbehind for swap cache folios.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 3/3] mm: zswap: drop cold writeback folios via swap dropbehind
series_items.patch_summary: This patch improves the zswap writeback process by dropping cold writeback folios via swap dropbehind. It addresses a problem where folios are left on the LRU for reclaim, wasting resources and keeping cold memory resident longer than necessary. The patch allocates the folio off the LRU, marks it PG_dropbehind to free it from the swap cache once writeback completes, and clears the PG_active flag after allocation to prevent issues with page freeing. This approach is a workaround until a fix for evaluating refaults on writeback buffers can be implemented.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch set extends the existing dropbehind mechanism to swap cache folios, allowing zswap to opt into it and free cold writeback folios promptly. Currently, when zswap writes an entry back, it allocates a folio and leaves it on the LRU for page reclaim to find and free later, wasting a reclaim scan and keeping cold memory resident longer than necessary. The patch set moves LRU insertion out of the swap cache allocator, drops dropbehind swap cache folios on writeback completion, and has zswap allocate its writeback folio off the LRU and mark it dropbehind to take advantage of this mechanism.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 1/2] mm: refactor find_next_best_node to find_next_best_node_in
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the find_next_best_node function to find_next_best_node_in, which takes an explicit candidates nodemask instead of always selecting from N_MEMORY. This change enables building fallback lists with non-N_MEMORY candidates without changing any existing functionality. The refactor is done by modifying three files: mm/internal.h, mm/memory-tiers.c, and mm/page_alloc.c. The patch has been reviewed and acknowledged by multiple kernel developers.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 2/2] mm/page_alloc: refactor build_node_zonelist() out of build_zonelists()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the code that builds zonelists in a node-ordered fashion, extracting it into a new function called build_node_zonelist(). This function takes a nodemask of candidate nodes and builds a zonelist for each selected node directly into the destination zonelist. The fallback order is printed as each node is added. The patch allows building new zonelists from candidate nodemasks instead of just the default N_MEMORY node state list, without introducing any functional changes.

Slight inaccuracy on the way zonelists are actually built.

Every node has a list in every zonelist.  The contents of each node's
list in that zonelist are limited to the candidate nodemask.

So consider the following nodes:  N0, N1, P2   (N=normal, P=private)

With the following candidate mappings:
   FALLBACK = N_MEMORY_GENERAL  (_COMMON)  (all normal nodes)
   PRIVATE  = N_MEMORY                     (all nodes)
   KTEST    = N_MEMORY & !N_MEMORY_GENERAL (only private nodes)

FALLBACK
  0  :  [0,1]
  1  :  [1,0]
  2  :  [0,1]  <- private node's fallback list is normal nodes

NOFALLBACK
  0  :  [0]
  1  :  [1]
  2  :  [2]

PRIVATE          Accessible via ALLOC_PRIVATE_ZONELIST
  0  :  [0,1,2]
  1  :  [1,0,2]
  2  :  [2,0,1]

  0  :  [0]
  1  :  [1]
  2  :  [2]

KTEST             Not accessible via any flag, completely isolated
  0  :  [2]
  1  :  [2]
  2  :  [2]

KTEST_NOFALLBACK  Not accessible via any flag, completely isolated
  0  :  []
  1  :  []
  2  :  [2]

allocator ktest-able.  Ktest is empowered to set the fallback list
directly rather than requiring a flag - not something any in-tree caller
can do - which lets it limit allocations to a private node and makes
mutations on the pgdat for that node deterministic from test-to-test.

Works on UML too, so testing is very fast. :]

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch refactors the zonelist constructors and iterators in the Linux kernel to make them more flexible and modular. The existing behavior of picking nodes from N_MEMORY is made explicit, allowing callers to narrow the set of nodes used for fallback lists. A new function find_next_best_node_in() takes a candidate set as an argument, making it easier to build zonelists over specific sets of nodes. Additionally, the per-node construction loop in build_zonelists() is extracted into a separate function build_node_zonelist(), which can be parameterized on the candidate nodemask and destination zonelist index. These changes enable more flexible and efficient management of zonelists, particularly for generating private node zonelists.

review_comments.summary: Author addressed Chris Li's concern that the counters are overloaded and can't express both limits, arguing that swap and zswap counters already work for this interaction and that memory.swap.max is a provisioning interface rather than an SLO limit. Author suggests that using pswap=swap would simplify things and implies that including zswap in swap is a bug.
sentiment_signals: author acknowledges a fix is needed
implies that current implementation has issues
review_comments.raw_body:
Possible, but arguably not needed. the swap and zswap counters already
work for this existing interaction.

As I pointed to in my response to Rik, in every reasonable use of
pswap+zswap the global swap counter is pointless.

So then pswap=swap and we're left with zswap and swap.

And I'm not convinced your reading of the swap counter as a limit on the
*logical* memory allowed to be swapped out is actually accurate.

  memory.swap.current
        The total amount of swap currently being used by the cgroup
        and its descendants.

  memory.swap.max
        Swap usage hard limit.  If a cgroup's swap usage reaches this
        limit, anonymous memory of the cgroup will not be swapped out.

There is no documentation I can find that has ever documented these
counters as "the amount of memory requiring a fault".  If you put a
compression system in front of physical swap - the counters as-described
would still be accurate, while your reading would be broken.

"swap" here is highly implied to mean "storage" as opposed to memory,
which is why "zswap" defines its limits in terms of memory.

  memory.zswap.current
        The total amount of memory consumed by the zswap compression
        backend.

  memory.zswap.max
        Zswap usage hard limit. If a cgroup's zswap pool reaches this
        limit, it will refuse to take any more stores before existing
        entries fault back in or are written out to disk.

If you're presently using swap.max to mean the "logical amount of memory
allowed to be swapped" - then your usage does not meet the definition of
the knob.  You need to justify that your use case cannot be expressed
via memory.min/low controls:

  memory.min
        Hard memory protection.  If the memory usage of a cgroup
        is within its effective min boundary, the cgroup's memory
        won't be reclaimed under any conditions. If there is no
        unprotected reclaimable memory available, OOM killer
        is invoked. Above the effective min boundary (or
        effective low boundary if it is higher), pages are reclaimed
        proportionally to the overage, reducing reclaim pressure for
        smaller overages.

That's an SLO interface.  memory.swap is a provisioning interface.

As it stands, I'm left viewing zswap's counter inclusion in swap as more
of a bug than a feature - they account for different things (memory vs
storage usage).

~Gregory

series_items.subject: [PATCH 1/8] nfsd: clear NFSD_NET_UP before dropping the generic resource reference
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a potential issue in the NFS server code where NFSD_NET_UP is left set after dropping the generic resource reference, causing inconsistencies when accessing host-wide file cache and NFSv4 tables. The fix involves clearing NFSD_NET_UP before dropping the reference to ensure that the bit never claims the resources are available once they may already be gone. This change does not introduce any functional changes but rather ensures a consistent state in the system.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 2/8] nfsd: make max_blksize a per-namespace setting
series_items.patch_summary: This patch makes the maximum block size a per-namespace setting in the NFS daemon, rather than a global module-scope variable. This change prevents containerized environments from leaking this value across namespaces and affecting other containers' payload sizes. The patch updates various files to reflect this change, including moving the max_blksize field into struct nfsd_net and updating functions that interact with it.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 3/8] nfsd: move the control plane to a per-namespace mutex
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the control plane of the NFS daemon (nfsd) to a per-namespace mutex, reducing serialization across network namespaces and improving performance. The global nfsd_mutex is retained for host-wide resources, while the new nn->nfsd_mutex handles namespace-specific data. This change allows for concurrent startup and shutdown of NFS services in different namespaces, reducing stalls and improving scalability.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 4/8] nfsd: rename nfsd_mutex to nfsd_global_mutex
series_items.patch_summary: This patch renames the global mutex in the NFS server code from 'nfsd_mutex' to 'nfsd_global_mutex'. The change is mechanical and does not affect functionality, but it clarifies which mutex a call site means by giving it a more descriptive name. This change affects several files in the NFS server code, including filecache.c, netns.h, nfsctl.c, nfsd.h, and nfssvc.c.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 5/8] nfsd: give the open file cache its own mutex
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new mutex, `nfsd_file_cache_mutex`, to protect the open file cache in the NFS server. The existing global mutex, `nfsd_global_mutex`, is left to handle only server start/stop operations, while the new mutex handles cache initialization and teardown, as well as reader and walker access to the cache. This change improves concurrency and reduces lock contention between unrelated namespaces.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 6/8] selftests/nfsd: factor the netlink plumbing into a shared header
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the generic-netlink plumbing code from nfsd_netlink_listener.c to a shared header file nfsd_netlink.h, making it reusable by other NFS selftests without adding extra dependencies. The code is refactored as static inline functions to ensure each test binary gets its own copy and there's nothing extra to link.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 7/8] selftests/nfsd: add cross-namespace isolation tests
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new test suite for the NFSD control plane's cross-namespace isolation. The tests verify that one namespace's settings and running server do not affect another namespace, ensuring that changes made to one namespace are isolated from others. The tests cover various aspects of NFSD behavior, including maximum block size, busy status, pool statistics, listener management, and file cache handling.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 8/8] selftests/nfsd: add a cross-namespace control-plane soak
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a self-test to the NFS daemon (NFSD) that exercises its control plane from multiple namespaces simultaneously, testing the lock nesting and synchronization between namespaces. The test creates multiple namespaces, each with an NFSD server, and has them churn through various operations that interact with host-wide locks, including starting and stopping servers, emptying listener sets, and reading file caches. The test also includes synchronized rounds where all namespaces attempt to transition from a 0->1 state at the same time, which is only possible after per-namespace locking stopped serializing namespaces against each other. The test asserts that the kernel does not warn or produce any lockdep splats, and it logs a note if lockdep looks absent. The test is designed to catch issues with lock nesting, serialization, and refcount saturation.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 2/3] mm/huge_memory: don't queue folios that can never be underused
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the handling of anonymous PMD-sized folios in the Linux kernel by skipping the queuing of folios that can never be underused, reducing unnecessary work and improving performance. The default khugepaged/max_ptes_none setting causes the shrinker to never split these folios for being underused, so they are not queued. This change is particularly important for a subsequent patch that adds anonymous mTHP folios to the deferred split list, as it prevents small mTHP orders from taking the list_lru lock on every anonymous fault.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 3/3] mm/memory: add anonymous mTHP folios to the deferred split list
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds anonymous mTHP (huge page) folios to the deferred split list in the Linux kernel's memory management code. The patch addresses a problem where fully mapped huge pages that are mostly zero-filled do not get split by the deferred split shrinker, leading to memory regressions. The solution involves mirroring the behavior for PMD-sized folios and adding a check to minimize overhead on common fault paths.

commit 5a9c05d86683db5449b7fefd278c461cffb55234
Author: Nico Pache <nico.pache@linux.dev>
Date:   Fri Jun 5 10:14:11 2026 -0600

    mm/khugepaged: generalize __collapse_huge_page_* for mTHP support

    generalize the order of the __collapse_huge_page_* and collapse_max_*
    functions to support future mTHP collapse.

    The current mechanism for determining collapse with the
    khugepaged_max_ptes_none value is not designed with mTHP in mind.  This
    raises a key design issue: if we support user defined max_pte_none values
    (even those scaled by order), a collapse of a lower order can introduces
    an feedback loop, or "creep", when max_ptes_none is set to a value greater
    than HPAGE_PMD_NR / 2.  [1]

    With this configuration, a successful collapse to order N will populate
    enough pages to satisfy the collapse condition on order N+1 on the next
    scan.  This leads to unnecessary work and memory churn.

    To fix this issue introduce a helper function that will limit mTHP
    collapse support to two max_ptes_none values, 0 and HPAGE_PMD_NR - 1.
    This effectively supports two modes: [2]

    - max_ptes_none=0: never collapses if it encounters an empty PTE or a PTE
      that maps the shared zeropage. Consequently, no memory bloat.
    - max_ptes_none=511 (on 4k pagesz): Always collapse to the highest
      available mTHP order.

    This removes the possibility of "creep", and a warning will be emitted if
    any non-supported max_ptes_none value is configured with mTHP enabled.
    Any intermediate value will default mTHP collapse to max_ptes_none=0.

    mTHP collapse will not honor the khugepaged_max_ptes_shared or
    khugepaged_max_ptes_swap parameters, and will fail if it encounters a
    shared or swapped entry.


Tracing back the discussion on that patch should give you all the details.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch removes the ALLOC_NON_BLOCK flag from the ALLOC_RESERVES definition in the Linux kernel's page allocation system. series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 01/11] mm, swap: add virtual swap device infrastructure
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces the virtual swap device infrastructure, which allows for dynamic allocation of swap clusters and enables the creation of a virtual swap device that can be used by vswap. The device is capped at approximately 8 TiB in size and uses a 64-bit architecture. The patch also includes changes to various kernel files to support the new infrastructure and adds a kernel parameter 'vswap' to control the behavior of the virtual swap device. The dynamic-cluster allocator is wired in, but no allocation path can select it yet, as this will be handled in subsequent patches.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 02/11] mm, swap: support zswap and zero-filled swap pages as vswap backends
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds support for virtual swap (vswap) using zswap and zero-filled swap pages as backends, allowing compressed or zero-filled pages to be stored without pre-allocating physical swap space. It introduces a new vswap layer that decouples PTE swap entries from physical backing, enabling efficient compression and detection of zero-filled pages. The patch also includes changes to handle virtual swap-backed entries in the zswap shrinker and writeback paths, as well as updates to mem_cgroup_can_swap() to account for vswap's contribution to memory pressure. Additionally, it introduces a new function mem_cgroup_can_vswap() to determine whether vswap is enabled for a given cgroup.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 03/11] mm, swap: prepare the swap IO path for vswap
series_items.patch_summary: This patch prepares the swap IO path for vswap by allowing it to submit IO for a swap entry other than folio->swap. It achieves this by computing the sector from an explicit entry, which is then used in various functions such as swap_add_folio and __swap_writeout. This change enables the batching path to serve both vswap entries and physical entries mapped directly into PTEs. The patch also updates ops->can_merge to measure sectors and byte offsets from the batch head plus accumulated length instead of from the previous folio plus its size.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 04/11] mm, swap: support physical swap as a vswap backend
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds support for physical swap as a backend for the virtual swap layer, allowing zswap to allocate physical slots on demand when it declines a page. It introduces a new mechanism to track physical slots via pointer-tagged swap_table entries and modifies readahead and swapoff operations to work with this new system. The patch also includes changes to handle cases where zswap is disabled or the folio's cgroup does not support vswap, bypassing vswap and mapping the slot directly into PTEs.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 05/11] mm, swap: enable THP swapin for vswap entries
series_items.patch_summary: This patch enables transparent huge page (THP) swapin for vswap entries, allowing large anonymous folios to be swapped in as a unit when their vswap entries share contiguous physical swap slots on a synchronous IO device. This change improves performance by reducing the number of faults and retries required during swap operations. The patch also introduces checks for zswap-backed or mixed-backing batches, which are still refused and fall back to order-0 faults. The approach taken involves modifying existing functions in the mm module to handle vswap entries and THP swapin.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 06/11] mm, swap: write back vswap zswap entries to physical swap
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds support for writing back zswap-backed vswap entries to physical swap. It mirrors the existing zswap writeback path, but allocates the backing physical slot on demand at writeback time rather than pre-allocating it. The zswap shrinker no longer skips vswap entries unless there is no available physical swap space. The patch modifies the zswap_writeback_entry function to handle vswap entries by allocating physical backing before decompressing and storing the entry in the vtable.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 07/11] mm, swap: reclaim physical slots backing cache-only vswap entries
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses an issue where physical slots backing cache-only vswap entries are not being reclaimed when they become redundant. When a vswap entry's swap_count drops to 0 while its folio is still in the swap cache, the entry becomes cache-only and its physical slot is no longer needed. However, the current implementation does not properly reclaim these slots. This patch introduces a new flag, SWP_RMAP_CACHE_ONLY, to indicate when a vswap entry is cache-only, and modifies the physical reclaim scanner to reclaim such slots once swap usage exceeds 50%. The reclaimed slots are then freed, allowing for new allocations.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 08/11] mm, swap: only charge physical swap entries
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies how memory charge is handled for swap entries in Linux. It ensures that only physical swap entries are charged against a cgroup's swap, rather than all swap entries including zswap-backed and zero-filled pages. This change affects the behavior of memory.swap.current and allows cgroups to reclaim their anon memory even when memory.swap.max is set to 0. The patch also refactors the swap memcg operations into separate helpers for getting, recording, charging, uncharging, and putting swap entries.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 09/11] mm, swap: add debugfs counters for vswap
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds two debugfs counters to track virtual swap usage in the Linux kernel. The first counter, 'used', tracks the number of virtual swap slots (pages) currently allocated. The second counter, 'alloc_reject', counts the cumulative pages that failed to get a vswap slot. These counters are exposed under the '/sys/kernel/debug/vswap/' directory and can be accessed via debugfs. This patch addresses the need for visibility into virtual swap usage statistics, which is useful for debugging and performance analysis.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 10/11] mm, swap: defer memcg_table allocation for physical swap clusters
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes memory allocation for physical swap clusters by deferring the allocation of a memcg table until it is actually needed. This reduces unnecessary memory usage in cases where a cluster only holds vswap backings, which do not require a memcg table. The patch modifies the swap_cluster_alloc_table function to allocate the memcg table eagerly only when the cluster is known to be used for direct mapping or when vswap is disabled.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v5 11/11] mm, swap: back vswap clusters with a VM_SPARSE array
series_items.patch_summary: This patch replaces the vswap cluster's individually allocated memory with a VM_SPARSE array, simplifying access and reducing overhead. The new approach eliminates per-cluster allocation, xarray nodes, and RCU grace periods, making it more efficient. The swap_cluster_info_dynamic wrapper is removed, and the virtual table for a vswap cluster is freed when it empties, reclaiming most of its memory. This change aims to improve performance and reduce memory usage in the Linux kernel's swap management.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series introduces Virtual Swap Space (vswap), a feature that allows Linux to use a portion of physical memory as swap space, improving performance and reducing the need for disk-based swap. The patches address various issues and cleanups, including overcommit guessing, swapfile size limits, and memcg private id refcnt saturation. Additionally, they refactor swap-related operations into composable building blocks and introduce a new data structure to replace the xarray. The series also includes several bug fixes and performance improvements.

series_items.patch_summary: This patch allows BPF (Berkeley Packet Filter) programs to defer memory.high enforcement, which prevents tasks holding kernel locks from being stuck in the charge path. It introduces high_policy ops that provide a read-only snapshot of the charge and allow programs to return a request. This approach enables more efficient handling of memory allocation and deallocation by allowing BPF programs to manage memory usage without blocking other tasks.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 4/4] selftests/bpf: add a cgroupfs lock-holder bpf_memcg_ops sample
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a BPF (Berkeley Packet Filter) sample to track and enforce policies on tasks holding cgroupfs kernfs locks. The policy, called bpf_memcg_ops, prevents tasks from being inline memory.high enforced if they hold such locks. It does this by tracking the depth of kernfs_rwsem and kernfs_supers_rwsem locks per task using fentry/fexit hooks. Two counters are used to guard against incorrect enforcement. The patch is measured to improve performance on a reproducer, reducing stall times and increasing throughput.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 1/3] kernfs: activate a new node without dropping kernfs_rwsem
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the kernfs kernel file system by reducing the number of write locks taken on a root directory when creating new nodes. It achieves this by calling the kernfs_activate_one function before dropping the lock, which only activates the newly created node without walking its children. This reduces the overhead of acquiring and releasing the write lock for every new node, resulting in improved performance. The patch also includes statistics showing a significant reduction in write lock acquisitions after applying the change.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 2/3] kernfs: allocate the new name outside kernfs_rwsem
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the kernfs_rename_ns function to allocate a duplicate of the new name outside of the kernfs_rwsem write lock. This is done by creating a copy of the new name before taking the lock and freeing it again if the rename operation does not need it. The goal of this change is to prevent a rename operation from entering reclaim while other operations in the hierarchy are waiting behind it, which could lead to deadlocks.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 3/3] kernfs: free the old name outside kernfs_rwsem
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the freeing of an old name in the kernfs_rename_ns function outside of the kernfs_rwsem write lock. The old name is already unpublished by the time it needs to be freed, so there's no need for it to happen under the lock. This change helps prevent potential deadlocks caused by holding the write lock while waiting out a grace period.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: The patch series aims to reduce the work done under the kernfs_rwsem write lock by reordering operations and allocating memory before acquiring the lock. This is achieved in three patches: (1) activating a new node without dropping the lock, (2) allocating the new name outside the lock, and (3) freeing the old name after unlocking.

Sorry about the delay.

On Sat, Sep 12, 2026 at 07:14:50PM -0700, Shakeel Butt wrote:
> kernfs_rwsem is per kernfs root, so sysfs and cgroupfs have one each for
> the whole machine, and every create, remove and rename takes it for
> writing.  Whatever a writer does while holding it, everyone else waits
> for.  These three patches take work out of that section.
> 
> Patch 1: kernfs_add_one() links the node in, drops the lock, then calls
> kernfs_activate(), which takes it again.  sysfs does not create nodes
> deactivated, so it pays two write locks for every file and directory.
> Activate before dropping the lock.  lock_stat says 1200 -> 830 write
> acquisitions for creating and destroying five dummy netdevs.
> 
> Patch 2: kernfs_rename_ns() calls kstrdup_const() under the lock.  It is
> the only GFP_KERNEL allocation under the write lock in kernfs, so a
> rename can enter reclaim with the lock held.  Allocate before the lock.
> 
> Patch 3: kernfs_rename_ns() also frees the old name under the lock with
> kfree_rcu_mightsleep().  When its batching allocation fails, which is
> what happens under memory pressure, it falls back to synchronize_rcu().
> A rename can then wait out a grace period with the lock held.  Free
> after the unlock.
> 
> Tested with the kernfs selftests under KASAN and lockdep.
